summary: This informational RFC reports on an IAB workshop, Interconnecting Smart Objects with the Internet, held in Prague on 25 March 2011. It gathered feedback on deploying IETF protocols in constrained environments and lists conclusions.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC records a one-day meeting where people who build and deploy small networked devices talked about what breaks when you run ordinary internet protocols on them. It lists what they agreed was still unsolved.

questions: interconnecting smart objects with the internet
what are the challenges of internet of things
how do constrained devices use protocols
what is the smart object workshop
subtitle: What a group of practitioners had to say about running ordinary internet protocols on devices with 2 KB of memory and a tiny battery.

tldr.problem: Small networked devices cannot run the protocols the internet was designed for without running out of battery, bandwidth, memory or money.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held a one-day workshop in Prague where researchers and developers described their experience of deploying IETF protocols in constrained environments.
tldr.outcome: It is a report rather than a specification. It records the constraints, the open architectural questions and a list of areas where the workshop thought more work was needed.

today: RFC 6574 is an Informational document published in April 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a report on a workshop held in Prague on 25 March 2011, and the RFC says the views it records are those of the participants and do not necessarily reflect the position of the Internet Architecture Board.

sections.title: What the Workshop Set Out to Find
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board holds occasional workshops on long-term issues and strategies for the internet, to suggest future directions. That planning role sits alongside the engineering work done in the IETF working groups.

Today's internet is experienced by users as a set of applications such as email, instant messaging and web services. These applications do not usually need the user to be present while they run, and the end devices that take part are generally assumed to have plenty of performance. But there are a large number of deployed embedded devices, and there is substantial value in connecting them to the internet. The term Internet of Things denotes the trend in which a large number of devices use communication services offered by the internet protocols. Many of these devices are not operated directly by people, but exist as components in buildings and vehicles, or are spread out in the environment, and they vary a lot in computing power, memory, electrical power and communications bandwidth.

Some of these devices have previously used proprietary networks and are now migrating to the internet protocol suite, so that one network can be shared between all the applications. Much of that development can simply run on existing protocols: home entertainment and monitoring systems often offer a web interface. In many cases the new constrained environments can also benefit from additional protocols and extensions that cut the communications and the computing needed, and the IETF working groups targeting them are the Constrained RESTful Environments, IPv6 over Low power WPAN, Routing Over Low power and Lossy networks, and the Light-Weight Implementation Guidance group.

The workshop explored what researchers and developers had learned about the characteristics of constrained devices. Engineers know that many design considerations have to be balanced when writing protocols and architectures, and balancing code size, economic incentives, power consumption, usability and security is often difficult. The scope covered constrained nodes and constrained networks, and the call for position papers asked for work in five areas: scalability, power efficiency, interworking between technologies and network domains, usability and manageability, and security and privacy.

The goal was to discuss the experience of deploying IETF protocols in constrained environments. As the organisers put it, running protocols such as IPv4, IPv6, UDP, TCP and HTTP on constrained devices is clearly possible, but protocol designers, system architects and developers still have to keep the limitations in mind. They were also looking for issues where implementers have no solution yet, or where researchers predict problems, and the workshop was meant to identify problems and discover common interests that might turn into new work or a change of direction in work already under way.

sections.title: What Constrained Means
sections.content:
Not all nodes suffer from the same set of limitations, and the workshop was spurred by the growing presence of constrained devices on the network.

Energy. Since wireless communication can be a large part of a wireless device's power budget, reducing unnecessary communication can significantly increase the battery life of a low-end device. The choice of low-power radio also affects overall energy consumption, as does sleeping periodically when the device is not in use, and some nodes wake only periodically to handle the communications they need. That is quite the opposite of the always-on paradigm of regular internet hosts, and even for devices that are not battery operated, power is a constraint in terms of energy efficiency goals.

Bandwidth. Low-power radio networks offer limited bandwidth and show high packet loss and high variability in link quality. The data rates vary from 20 to 900 kilobits per second, as in IEEE 802.15.4, and nodes may be used in usually highly unstable radio environments. The physical-layer packet size may be limited to around 100 bytes.

Memory. The amount of volatile and persistent storage affects how programs execute and has important implications for what a protocol stack can do. The Arduino UNO board, for example, gives a developer 2 KB of RAM and 32 KB of flash memory, with no extensions such as microSD cards.

Processor and size. A system designer also has to think about processor constraints, which often relate to energy ones, since a lower-performance processor consumes less energy. The design of the mainboard may allow components to be put to sleep to lower consumption further. Embedded systems are purpose built with only the hardware the task needs, while general-purpose personal computers are less constrained and offer many optional plug-in peripherals. The intended environment matters too: a humidity sensor deployed outside a building may need to work from -50 to +85 degrees Celsius. Size is limited as well: traditional mainboards such as the ATX design, 305 by 244 mm, or the mini-ITX design found in home theatre PCs, 170 by 170 mm, are much larger than embedded layouts such as CoreExpress at 58 by 65 mm, and the sensors, peripherals, power adapter or battery and case all have to be accounted for. Cost restrictions apply on top of all of this.

Things get harder when the network nodes are constrained as well as the hosts. While there are constant improvements, Moore's law is less effective in the embedded space than in personal computing: gains from more transistors are more likely to be spent on cutting cost and power than on raising computing power.
sections.plainLanguage: Small devices are short of everything: battery, bandwidth, memory, space and money. The RFC lists the numbers, including a board with 2 KB of memory and radio links that carry around 100 bytes at a time at between 20 and 900 kilobits per second.

sections.title: One Internet, or Separate Networks?
sections.content:
Devices that used to live on proprietary or application-specific networks are now migrating to IP networks, but it is not clear that they are on the same IP network as everything else. Controlled applications such as the fountains in front of the Bellagio hotel in Las Vegas, which run as a distributed control system, probably do not exchange their control messages over the same network the hotel's guests use for their internet traffic, and the same argument has been made for smart grids, which are described as digitally enabled electrical grids that gather, distribute and act on information about the behaviour of all participants in order to improve the efficiency, reliability, economics and sustainability of electricity services. The question raised at the workshop is therefore in what sense we are talking about one internet, or about using IP technology for a separate walled garden that is independent of the internet.

Cullen Jennings compared the position with the evolution of voice over IP: at first many vendors recommended running it over a separate VLAN or separate infrastructure, and nobody could see how to make the real-time guarantees, how to debug it, or how to get it to work, because the internet is not ideally suited to guarantees for real-time systems. Over time people got better at making voice work across that kind of network, and they then noticed that having voice on a separate virtual network from their other applications was a disaster: they could not decide whether a machine was running a softphone and whether its traffic went on a voice or a data network. At that point they realised they needed a converged network and all moved to one. He expected the same here: at first very separated networks, then running over the same hardware to take advantage of not having to deploy several sets of wires around buildings, and over time strong needs to communicate directly. The system should be designed for the long run, on the assumption that everything ends up on the same network even if it is planned to start on separate ones.

It is clearly possible to let sensors in a building talk through the wireless access points and the same infrastructure used for internet access, and those who want separation at the physical layer can have it too. What matters is that the different deployment philosophies do not force a loss of interoperability. Ralph Droms put the other side of the argument: the level of interoperability that IP achieved fostered innovation at the application layer, and bright people will take a phone, build an application, and connect it with the appropriate security controls to the things in their house in ways nobody had thought about before. Otherwise, the argument goes, we are just building another telephone network.

Domain-specific stacks and profiles. Imagine a building network where a new light bulb should, out of the box and without further configuration, interoperate with a light switch from a different vendor in the same room. That level of interoperability is not reached by network-layer interoperability alone: even running the same transport protocol and application protocol such as HTTP is not enough, because both devices have to understand the semantics of a payload meaning turn the light on. Standardising the whole stack for that scenario is possible, with IPv6 and a specific address configuration mechanism such as stateless address autoconfiguration, a network access authentication mechanism such as PANA, a service discovery mechanism such as multicast DNS with DNS-Based Service Discovery, an application-layer protocol such as CoAP over UDP, and the syntax and meaning of the light on and off functionality. But that is already a fair amount of agreement between stakeholders, and as the interactions get more complex the choices multiply: IPv4 and IPv6 at the network layer, several transport options such as UDP, TCP, SCTP and DCCP, and many choices at the application layer for communication protocols, data formats and data models. Different requirements have already produced client-server protocols in the style of HTTP, publish-subscribe protocols such as SIP and XMPP, and store-and-forward messaging borrowed from the delay tolerant networking community, each with its own identity and security mechanisms.

With the smart object constraints, it feels natural to develop such stacks, since each application domain, such as healthcare, smart grids or building networking, has its own requirements and its own community involved in the design. The questions the workshop raised are how likely these profiles are to be the right match for the future, how many of them there will be, whether the differences come only from the different requirements or also from the preferences of the people designing them, and how many stacks a multipurpose device has to implement. Standardising a profile for each application is not the only option: another is a common foundation, a protocol stack that every device implements and every application uses, which requires the different application domains to be analysed for their common characteristics, and how hard that agreement is depends on how many layers the foundation covers and how lightweight it has to be. The workshop found the available options not ideal, and said further discussion was needed.

Which layer? The end-to-end principle says functionality should be in the end points rather than the network, and an equally important recommendation is to put functionality higher in the protocol stack. The wide range of application requirements has led to a model where lower layers offer only very basic functionality and more sophisticated features are provided by the applications. There has nevertheless been a persistent desire to push application-layer functionality down into the lower layers, on the belief that performance improves. That functionality may take the form of a gateway, which bridges technologies, acts on behalf of other nodes and offers more generic services such as name-based routing and caching. Two examples of network-layer functionality were discussed: location, where giving each node a sense of proximity, such as being in the same room as the light switch, is not possible without manual configuration because routers can only tell whether other nodes share a subnet or provide coordinates, and widespread deployment of location awareness has not happened; and name-based routing, where the clean slate proposals such as named data networking let developers name equipment with human-readable identifiers that may change after a rehearsal, which raises scalability questions about variable-length names. The participants could not agree on what functionality should move from the application layer into the network layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Should a smart building run on the same network as everything else, or on a separate one? The room split, and the report's conclusion was to design for the long run where everything converges. It also asked whether a whole protocol stack should be standardised for each kind of device.

sections.title: Sleeping Nodes and the Cost of Staying Awake
sections.content:
One limitation of smart objects is their available energy. To extend the life of a watch battery or a single AAA battery for months, these low-power devices have to sleep 99% to 99.5% of the time. A light sensor may only wake up to check whether it is night so it can turn the bulbs on. Most of the system, particularly the communications components such as the wireless radio interface, is put into a sleeping state, and selected components such as sensors periodically check for relevant events and, if necessary, switch on other hardware. Every bit is precious, as is every round trip and every millisecond of radio activity.

Many IETF protocols are implicitly designed to be always on: the implementation waits for and reacts to incoming messages, and may maintain session state at various layers. Those protocols work well when energy is not a concern and when sending and receiving messages are cheap. It should be understood that energy is consumed in transmitting messages, and often more importantly in keeping the receiver awake. Letting devices sleep most of the time preserves energy but creates real challenges for protocol design.

The inherent problem for a stationary node resuming from sleep is that another node may have taken its address while it was away. A number of steps are needed before it can send a packet, and a new address may have to be obtained, for example with DHCP or stateless address autoconfiguration. Optionally, Detecting Network Attachment procedures can shorten the setup time by noticing that the node is using the same default gateway. For a mobile node that was sleeping, it may have moved to another network, a sleeping laptop carried to a new environment, and on resumption it may find that its address has become invalid.

Four design considerations follow. Rethink the always-on assumption. Where a protocol assumes nodes are always on, alternatives have to be considered: dropping functionality, such as not implementing Detecting Network Attachment or duplicate address detection, or using a sleep proxy. Sleep proxies let periodic messages be sent on behalf of sleeping nodes, but that approach assumes the energy constraints do not apply to the proxy, which may not hold if the whole network is deployed in the field without power. Another option is for devices to state their sleep cycles explicitly, so they only check for messages periodically, measured in milliseconds, seconds or hours, which is the approach IEEE 802.11 takes with its energy conservation mechanisms.

Reduce network attachment costs. Obtaining an address and assuring its uniqueness can be costly, and in a network where nodes spend much of their time asleep but are not necessarily mobile, are all of those procedures really necessary? Ways of reducing the number of protocol interactions without sacrificing correctness would help. The main focus of past investigations has been on IPv6 and neighbour discovery, but other protocols deserve a deeper look too, such as DNS and DHCP.

Avoid verbose protocols. Protocols that need several round trips, or that use lengthy messages with verbose encodings such as XML, are not always suited to constrained environments. A low-power node using a verbose protocol has to spend more energy sending the message and has to stay powered on for longer while it waits for the exchange to finish. The best fix is to design the protocols so the simplest possible exchanges are used, and alternative encodings and compression may help in some cases.

Think about system-wide efficiency. Energy efficiency matters for other devices too, including laptops, desktops and phones, but where the goal is overall energy use rather than battery life for low-power devices, the total consumption of all the elements has to be considered. In a home, a light bulb using internet technology may use little power, but the device controlling it may use a lot, so the two, and possibly many others, have to be considered together.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that sleeps 99% of the time has to redo its network setup every time it wakes, which costs energy. The RFC lists four ways to design protocols that assume devices are asleep most of the time.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
As with any other protocol solution, security has to be considered early in the design of a smart object application, and the recommendations for IETF protocol architects, such as those in RFC 3552 and RFC 4101, apply here too. There are additional constraints, but security has to be a mandatory part of the solution, with the hope of implementations that provide security features, deployments that use them, and finally the use of better security mechanisms. The lack of direct user interaction places hard requirements on deployment models, configuration mechanisms, and software upgrade and crypto-agility mechanisms.

Because many security mechanisms allow customisation, particularly over the cryptographic primitives used, many believe the IETF security solutions are usable without modification across much of the smart object domain. Others call for new work on cryptographic primitives that use a single primitive, such as AES, as the building block for all cryptographic functions, because the benefit would be a smaller overall footprint, especially given the hardware limits of some embedded devices, whose architecture prevents pipelining from being used. In the excitement about optimisation, other factors matter too: widespread support in libraries, and intellectual property rights. The difficulty of deploying elliptic curve cryptography is partly attributable to its IPR situation, and reusing libraries that provide cryptographic functions is clearly an important way of using available memory more efficiently. To deal with performance and footprint, moving resource-hungry functions to parties with more cryptographic power has been considered, for example delegating certificate validation to servers, which the IETF has standardised before, for the Online Certificate Status Protocol in IKEv2 and in TLS.

Focusing only on the cryptographic primitives would be shortsighted, and many would argue that it is the easy part. Key management and credential enrolment are considered a big challenge, particularly where usability requirements have to be taken into account. Privacy raises another group of challenges: with smart grids, some have voiced concern about the ability of third parties to keep track of an individual's energy consumption and draw conclusions from it, and it is easy to see how a scale connected to the internet to upload weight information to a social network could raise privacy concerns. The security mechanisms that protect the communication between parties also give some privacy protection, but they are clearly not enough to answer all of these concerns, and additional safeguards are needed even with the best communication security and access control in place.

Better deployment of security protocols across the whole internet would be very desirable, but practical considerations about usability and the incentives of the stakeholders involved have often led to slower adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: Security has to be built in from the start, and the hard parts are not the encryption but the key management and the privacy: a smart meter that reports your electricity use says a lot about you.

sections.title: Routing and the Work That Followed
sections.content:
Routing. A smart object network may also use routers under the same constraints as the end devices. Two approaches were under consideration for these low-power and lossy networks: mesh-under, which places routing functions at the link layer, so that all devices appear as immediate neighbours at the network layer, and route-over, where routing is done in the IP layer and not at all at the link layer, so that each physical hop appears as a single IP hop, ignoring devices that merely extend the range of the signalling such as repeaters. Routing here means running a routing protocol, and the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks, RPL, belongs to the route-over category.

Several architectural questions follow from where routing is provided. Protocols often assume that link characteristics are predictable for any device on the same link, yet latency, throughput and reliability may vary a lot between devices several link-layer hops away, so what timeout should be used, and what happens if a device is unreachable. With default router selection, two advertised routers may be a different number of hops away, so a device may need visibility into the path to decide, and it is not clear what path characteristics would be useful. Scoped message delivery to a neighbouring IP hop through link-local addressing lets some IP protocols talk to their immediate neighbours and so scope their recipients, and a link-local multicast message is received by every node in the same link-local realm unless the link layer provides special optimisations. And when path computation is done at the link layer as well as the network layer, what coordination is needed between the two.

Where several link-layer technologies are involved, routing at layer 3 has to be provided in any case, and those deciding on a deployment have to work out how to connect the smart objects to the internet infrastructure, with several wired and wireless technologies possibly suitable, and then decide between mesh-under and route-over and choose a routing protocol.

The IETF formed the Routing Over Low power and Lossy networks working group in 2008 to specify a routing solution for smart object environments. In its first year it studied the routing requirements in detail and surveyed a number of existing routing protocols, including AODV-style protocols, against them. That survey was inconclusive and was abandoned without producing an RFC. The group concluded that a new routing protocol was needed, and the work on RPL began as the IETF routing protocol for smart object networks. The document notes that controversial arguments about which routing protocol is best in a given environment are still going on, with Thomas Clausen arguing for an AODV-like protocol.

Conclusions and next steps. The workshop exposed participants to applications and their requirements, to radically different architectures and their problems, to existing technology seen from a new angle, and to details of the protocol stack and implementation experience. One goal was to identify areas needing further investigation, and the list reflects what the participants said on the day; it concerns potential work by the IETF and the IRTF, and the order implies no preference.

On security, the difficulty is that security-related exchanges and the computing they need contribute significantly to overall processing, so improving performance without lowering the security level remains a challenge, and the security needs of smart objects have to be balanced against the interoperability requirements of ordinary internet hosts, since different suites of algorithms tend to be chosen for the two environments. That is a trade-off between performance on the smart objects and end-to-end security, and solutions that mandate a trusted middlebox whose only job is to terminate security associations are frowned on from a security point of view, especially as end users of challenged devices are unlikely to understand the security consequences. The three recommendations were to investigate usability in cryptographic protocol design with regard to credential management, mentioning the Bluetooth pairing mechanism as a simple and reasonably secure way of introducing devices to a new environment, and noting that the IETF Credential and Provisioning working group was terminated prematurely for lack of progress, though its mailing list archive survives; to survey the standardised authentication and key exchange mechanisms for suitability in smart object environments, in terms of message size, computing, number of messages, code size and main memory requirements, with IKEv2 as a starting point and the Light-Weight Implementation Guidance working group as a venue; and to do research into lightweight cryptographic primitives, that is block ciphers, stream ciphers and hash functions, with the SHA-3 competition and the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group as the forums.

The document warns that the difficulty and impact of choosing specialised algorithms for smart objects should not be underestimated: the extra specification complexity, since TLS already has hundreds of cipher suites defined and most are unused in practice; the long latency in roll-out, since many hosts are still using algorithms deprecated five to ten years ago; and the barriers that IPR-encumbered schemes place on widespread deployment. Any such algorithm would have to offer very significant benefits to be adopted, and 20% less CPU usage is unlikely to be a winning argument.

The remaining topics named for further work were energy design, with discussion encouraged on a mailing list; information and content centric networking, where the work was not yet ready for standardisation and the formation of an IRTF research group had been proposed; architectural guidelines, suggesting the IAB write a document on what the current protocols can do and how the pieces combine; network management, starting a discussion of running NETCONF on smart objects; congestion control, asking whether it belongs in the transport protocol or the application protocol, with work on CoAP as a starting point; data models, since standardising application protocols does not by itself let a light switch and a light bulb interact; building networking, which led to the creation of the Home Networking working group after the workshop; discovery, with extensions to multicast DNS to work across multiple subnets, which smart object networks often use; and routing, where the work should start on multi-link subnetworks to mitigate renumbering as radio conditions change, and where the applicability of specific routing protocols needs further investigation.
sections.plainLanguage: The report ends with a work list. On routing it says the choice between putting routing in the radio layer and in the IP layer is still argued about, and on the algorithm side it warns that a small efficiency gain is not worth the deployment trouble a new algorithm causes.

viz.caption: THE FOUR DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS FOR ENERGY EFFICIENCY

cells: Drop functionality, or have devices state their sleep cycles so they only check periodically
Cut the number of protocol interactions without sacrificing correctness
Fewer round trips and shorter encodings, since each one costs energy
Count the energy used by the controller as well as by the device
